title: Proof
body_md:
We start the argument with an important consequence of \eqref{Sv}. We fix $\zeta \in S$ and let $S_{N(\zeta)} V_\zeta^\perp \subset T_\zeta S$ be the image of of $V_\zeta^\perp$ under $S_{N(\zeta)}$; $S_{N(\zeta)} V_\zeta^\perp$ is itself a subspace. We will make use of two projectors: $\pi_{V_\zeta^\perp}: T_\zeta S \rightarrow V_\zeta^\perp$, the orthogonal projector onto $V_\zeta^\perp$, and  $\pi_\zeta: T_\zeta S \rightarrow S_{N(\zeta)} V_\zeta^\perp$, the orthogonal projection onto $S_{N(\zeta)} V_\zeta^\perp$.
 
 
We claim that there exists $c_1 > 0$ such that the following holds true:
\begin{equation} \label{wecon}
| \pi_{\zeta} e | \geq c_1 |e|
\end{equation} 
for any $e \in V_\zeta^\perp$. We argue by contradiction: assume \eqref{wecon} is false. This implies the existence of a unit vector $e \in V_\zeta^\perp$
such that $|e \cdot S_{N(\zeta)} v| < c_1 |S_{N(\zeta)} v| \leq c_1 \nu_0 |v|, \forall v \in V_\zeta^\perp$.  Using the symmetry of $S_{N(\zeta)}$ we obtain $| S_{N(\zeta)} e \cdot  v| <  c_1 \nu_0 |v|, \forall v \in V_\zeta^\perp$, which implies $|\pi_{V_\zeta^\perp} S_{N(\zeta)} e| < c_1 \nu_0$. Let $w = S_{N(\zeta)} e- \pi_{V_\zeta^\perp} S_{N(\zeta)} e$. This vector has the following properties:

\begin{itemize}
    \item $w \in V_\zeta$;
    
    \item Its size is bounded below by
    \[
    |w|^2= | S_{N(\zeta)} e|^2- |\pi_{V_\zeta^\perp} S_{N(\zeta)} e|^2 > \nu_0^2 - c_1^2 \nu_0^2,
    \]
    and above by
    \[
    |w|^2= | S_{N(\zeta)} e|^2- |\pi_{V_\zeta^\perp} S_{N(\zeta)} e|^2 \leq  | S_{N(\zeta)} e|^2 \leq \nu_0^2;
    \]

    \item It also satisfies
    \[
    | S_{N(\zeta)} e \wedge w|= |\pi_{V_\zeta^\perp} S_{N(\zeta)} e| \cdot |w| \leq c_1 \nu_0^2.  
    \]
\end{itemize}

Thus we obtain a contradiction with \eqref{Sv} provided that $c_1 \nu_0^2 <  \nu_0 ( \nu_0^2 - c_1^2 \nu_0^2)^\frac12$; obviously this is achievable if $c_1 >0$ is chosen small enough in \eqref{wecon}. 

We now return to the proof of the main statements in our theorem. We make two simplifying assumptions: there exists $\zeta_0 \in S$ such that $N(\zeta_0) \in \mathcal H$ and that $\mathcal H^\perp \subset V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$. If the first assumption fails, we modify $\mathcal{H}$ by $O(\nu_0 \mu)$ to achieve it (unless the set $\tilde S$ is void in which case there is nothing to prove). If the second assumption fails we work with 
$\pi_{V_{\zeta_0}^\perp} e_1,..., \pi_{V_{\zeta_0}^\perp} e_m$ in the argument below instead of $ e_1,..., e_m$ . 

Let $e_1,...,e_m$ be an orthonormal base in $\mathcal H^\perp$. Since $N_0=N(\zeta_0) \in \mathcal H$ and $e_1,...,e_m$ are all perpendicular to $\mathcal H$, they are perpendicular to $N(\zeta_0)$ and therefore $e_1,...,e_m \in T_{\zeta_0} S$. 

Our first claim is that $(\mathcal N)^{-1}(\mathcal H):= \{ \zeta \in S: N(\zeta) \in \mathcal H \}$ is a submanifold of $S$ of codimension $m$, thus effectively identifying $\tilde S'$.  To do so it is convenient to work in a system of coordinates. 

We let $\pi_0=\pi_{\zeta_0}: T_{\zeta_0} S \rightarrow S_{N(\zeta_0)} V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$ be the orthogonal projection defined above. We first note the following
\begin{equation} \label{pi0e}
|\pi_0 e_i \wedge \mathcal H | \gtrsim 1, \quad \forall i=1,...,m.
\end{equation}
If this were not the case, then, since $e_i \in \mathcal H^\perp$, $|\pi_0 e_i \cdot e_i| \ll 1$ and this would be in contradiction with \eqref{wecon}. 

Now, for every $i \in \{1,...,m \}$ we have that $\pi_0 e_i \in  S_{N(\zeta_0)} V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$, therefore there exists $\tilde e_i \in V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$ with the property
$S_{N(\zeta_0)} \tilde e_i = \nu_0 \pi_0 e_i$; we add the factor $\nu_0$ so that $|\tilde e_i| \approx 1$, which we prove below. At first $\tilde e_i$ is uniquely determined modulo $\ker S_{N(\zeta_0)}$; however 
\eqref{Sv} implies $\ker S_{N(\zeta_0)} \cap V_{\zeta_0}^\perp=\emptyset$, and this makes the choice of $\tilde e_i$ unique within $V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$.

Next we establish that the system $\{\tilde e_i\}_{i=1,...,m}$ has good transversality properties. From \eqref{Sv} we have $c \nu_0 |\tilde e_i| \leq |S_{N_{\zeta_0}} \tilde e_i|= \nu_0 |\pi_0 e_i| \leq \nu_0 |e_i|= \nu_0$, therefore
\begin{equation} \label{elen}
|\tilde e_i| \leq c^{-1}, \quad \forall i=1,...,m.
\end{equation}
The set of vectors $\{ \tilde e_i\}_{i=1,...,m}$ is transversal in the following sense: there exists $\tilde c > 0$ (universal, independent of $\nu_0$) such that 
\begin{equation} \label{etrans}
|\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge \tilde e_m| \geq \tilde c. 
\end{equation}
 We assume the above is false, that is $|\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge \tilde e_m| < \tilde c$ and we establish that if $\tilde c$ is chose small enough then we run into a contradiction. We claim that 
 \[
 |S_{N(\zeta_0)}\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge S_{N(\zeta_0)} \tilde e_m| \lesssim  \nu_0^m |\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge \tilde e_m|. 
 \]
 This is a consequence of the fact that $\nu_0^{-1} S_{N(\zeta_0)}: V_{\zeta_0}^\perp \rightarrow S_{N(\zeta_0)} V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$ is a linear operator whose matrix has determinant $\approx 1$; indeed we have $|\nu_0^{-1} S_{N(\zeta_0)} v| \approx |v|, \forall v \in V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$. 
 
  Therefore $|S_{N(\zeta_0)}\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge S_{N(\zeta_0)} \tilde e_m| \lesssim \tilde c \nu_0^m$, and 
 $|\pi_0 e_1 \wedge .. \wedge \pi_0 e_m| \lesssim \tilde c$. Using \eqref{wecon} we obtain
 $|\frac{\pi_0 e_1}{|\pi_0 e_1|} \wedge .. \wedge \frac{\pi_0 e_m}{|\pi_0 e_m|}|  \lesssim \tilde c$. Using Lemma \ref{volc} it follows that there is a unit vector $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^m$ such that the size of
 $e=\alpha_1 \frac{e_1}{|\pi_0 e_1|} +..+\alpha_k \frac{e_m}{|\pi_0 e_m|}$ satisfies $|\pi_0 e| \lesssim \tilde c^\frac1m$.
  On the other hand, 
 \[
 |e|^2= \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\alpha_i^2}{|\pi_0 e_i|^2} \geq  1,
 \]
 while from \eqref{wecon} it follows that $|\pi_0 e| \gtrsim 1$. Thus if $\tilde c$ is small enough we obtain a contradiction. This establishes \eqref{etrans}. 
  
 \eqref{elen} and \eqref{etrans} imply that  we have produced a system of vectors with $|\tilde e_i| \approx 1, i=1,...,m$ and $|\tilde e_1 \wedge .. \wedge \tilde e_m| \gtrsim 1$. We can complete
this with a basis $\{\tilde e_i\}_{i=1,...,n-1}$ in $T_{\zeta_0} S$ with similar properties; indeed take $\{e_{m+1},...,e_{n-1}\}$ to be an orthornormal basis
to the $(span(\tilde e_1,...,\tilde e_m))^\perp$, the normal subspace to the subspace spanned by $\tilde e_1,..., \tilde e_m$. 

Since $N(\zeta_0) \perp T_{\zeta_0} S$, we also obtain a basis of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ by adding $N_0=N(\zeta_0)$ to the system $\{\tilde e_i\}_{i=1,...,n-1}$. 
We let $\pi_{N_0}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be the projector along $N_0$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ which is identified with $T_{\zeta_0} S$ and where
$\{\tilde e_i\}_{i=1,...,n-1}$ forms a basis. We define the parametrization of $S$ by simply projecting $S$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ along $N_0$;  this is a good parametrization in that it obeys \eqref{smooth}. We let $U$ be the image of $S$ under this parametrization, that is $U=\pi_{N_0}(S)$. In $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ we use coordinates $(\xi_1,...,\xi_{n-1})$ with the convention that $\xi_{1}, .., \xi_{n-1}$ are the coordinates in the directions of $\tilde e_1,..., \tilde e_{n-1}$ respectively; a apparent drawback of this system of coordinates is that is not Cartesian since $\tilde e_1,..., \tilde e_m$ is not an orthonormal system, but this plays no role in our analysis.  We define 
$\xi_0=\pi_{N_0}(\zeta_0)$. The parametrization of $S$ is given by $\Sigma: U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$ where $(\pi_{N_0} \circ \Sigma) (\xi)=\xi, \forall \xi \in U$. 
$(\mathcal N)^{-1}(\mathcal H)$ is given by the set of equations
\[
N(\Sigma(\xi))\cdot e_i=0, \quad \forall i=1,...,m. 
\]
We define $F: U \subset \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m, F=(F_1,...,F_m)$ by $F_i(\xi): = N(\Sigma(\xi)) \cdot e_i, \forall i=1,...,m$ 
and aim to solve the equation $F(\xi)=0$. This is done using the implicit function theorem and for this purpose we compute
\[
\frac{D(F_1,...,F_m)}{D(\xi_1,...,\xi_m)} (\xi_0)= \det [S_{N(\Sigma(\xi_0))} \tilde e_i \cdot e_j]_{i,j=1,...,m} = \det [\pi_0 e_i \cdot e_j]_{i,j=1,...,m}.
\]
The matrix $[\pi_0 e_i \cdot e_j]_{i,j=1,...,m}$ is symmetric because $\pi_0$ is a symmetric operator. Our goal is to prove that 
\[
|\det [\pi_0 e_i \cdot e_j]_{i,j=1,...,m}| \gtrsim 1. 
\]
Assume by contradiction that $|\det [\pi_0 e_i \cdot e_j]_{i,j=1,...,m}| \ll 1$. 
By Lemma \ref{vols} part ii), there exists $\alpha=(\alpha_1,...,\alpha_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ a unit vector such that 
\[
|(\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i \pi_0 e_i \cdot e_j)_{j=1,...,m}| \ll 1.
\]
We let $e=\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i  e_i$ be the unit vector in $(\mathcal H)^\perp$ and conclude that $|(\pi_0 e \cdot e_j)_{j=1,...,m}| < \tilde \nu_3^\frac1m$.
From this we further estimate
\[
|\pi_0 e \cdot e| \leq \sum_{i=1}^m |\alpha_i| |\pi_0 e \cdot e_i| \leq |\alpha| |(\pi_0 e \cdot e_j)_{j=1,...,m}| \ll 1,
\]
and conclude with $|\pi_0 e|^2 = |\pi_0 e \cdot \pi_0 e|= |\pi_0^2 e \cdot  e|= |\pi_0 e \cdot  e | \ll 1$. On the other hand,
from \eqref{wecon} we have $|\pi_0 e|^2 \gtrsim  |e|^2=1$, thus we obtain a contradiction.  

We can invoke the implicit function theorem to conclude that there exists an open neighborhood $U' \subset U$ of $\xi_0$ and 
$\Sigma': U' \cap \mathbb{R}^{n-m-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ such that
\[
\Sigma^{-1} (\mathcal N)^{-1}(\mathcal H) \cap U'=\{ (\Sigma'_1(\xi_{m+1},...,\xi_{n-1}), .., \Sigma'_m(\xi_{m+1},...,\xi_{n-1}), \xi_{m+1},...,\xi_{n-1}\}.
\]
This gives us the correct structure for $S'=\Sigma^{-1} (\mathcal N)^{-1}(\mathcal H) \cap U'$. 
The size of the neighborhood $U'$ of $\xi_0$ is uniform with respect to the choice of $\xi_0$ since it depends on parameters for which we have uniform bounds across $S$, see \eqref{smooth}, \eqref{Sv} and \eqref{wecon}; to be more precise, the result gives $U'=B_r(\xi_0) \cap U$ and the size of $r$ is uniform with respect to the choice of $\xi_0$. If we assume that the diameter of $S$ is small enough, then $U=\pi_{N_0}(S) \subset B_r(\xi_0)$
and the local solution becomes the global one.

From the above analysis it also follows that $\tilde S'=\Sigma(S')$ is a submanifold of $S$ of codimension $m$.

Next we prove that $\tilde S$ belongs to the correct neighborhood of $\tilde S'$. To do so, it suffices to prove that $\pi_{N_0} \tilde S \subset B_{\tilde \mu} S'$,
for some $\tilde \mu \lesssim \mu$. We rely on the fact that the system $\{ \tilde e_i \}_{i=1,...,m}$ is transversal to $S'$.  We fix $\xi \in S'$, fix $i \in \{1,...,m\}$, and let $\gamma(t)=\xi+t \tilde e_i \in U, |t| \ll 1$; the range of $t$ is constrained by the size of $U$
since we impose $\gamma(t) \in U$. We have
\[
\begin{split}
N(\Sigma(\gamma(t)))-N(\Sigma(\gamma(0))) & = \int_{0}^{t} S_{N(\gamma(s))} d\Sigma(\gamma(s)) \gamma'(s) ds  \\
& = t S_{N(\gamma(0))} d\Sigma(\gamma(0)) \gamma'(0) + \nu_0 o(t) \\
&= t S_{N(\zeta_0)} d\Sigma(\xi_0) \tilde e_i + \nu_0 o(t)  \\
&=  t \nu_0 \pi_0 e_i + \nu_0 o(t). 
\end{split}
\]
In the above we used the following straightforward facts:  $d\Sigma(\xi_0)=Id$, $\|S_{N(\gamma(0))}-S_{N(\zeta_0)} \| \ll \nu_0$ (a consequence of \eqref{sm23}) and 
$\|d\Sigma(\gamma(0))-d\Sigma(\xi_0)\| \ll 1$; the last two inequalities involve matrix norms and use the small diameter property of $S$. 

From \eqref{wecon} and \eqref{pi0e}, we have that $|\pi_0 e_i| \gtrsim 1$ and $| \pi_0 e_i \wedge \mathcal H| \gtrsim 1$; since $N(\Sigma(\gamma(0))) \in \mathcal H$,
it follows that a necessary condition of $\Sigma(\gamma(t)) \in \tilde S$ is that $|t| \lesssim \mu $. 
Since the system $\{ \tilde e_i \}_{i=1,...,m}$ is transversal to $S'$, whose co-dimension is $m$, it follows that $\pi_{N_0} \tilde S \subset B_{\tilde \mu} S'$,
for some $\tilde \mu \lesssim \mu$. 



As for ii), we notice that any unit vector $n \in N_\zeta$ has the property that its projection on the $span\{ \tilde e_1,...,\tilde e_m \} \subset V_{\zeta_0}^\perp$ 
has length bounded from below by a universal constant; this simply follows from the structure of $\tilde S'$ and the smallness of the diameter of all submanifolds involved. As a consequence $|n \wedge V_{\zeta_0}^\perp| \gtrsim 1$, thus $|n \wedge V_{\zeta}^\perp| \gtrsim 1$. This implies that $|N_\zeta \wedge V_\zeta| \gtrsim 1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The estimate follows immediately from Theorem \ref{mainTd}, once we check the curvature conditions \eqref{Scurv} and \eqref{curvad} with the correct numerology.

It is convenient to use spherical coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$ in this argument, due to the radial symmetry of the paraboloid. In particular, the paraboloid is parametrized as
\begin{align*}
    \varphi(r,\theta,\phi)=(r\cos(\theta)\sin(\phi), r\sin(\theta)\sin(\phi), r\cos(\phi), r^2)\in\mathbb{R}^4.
\end{align*}
The tangent plane at any point $\zeta=(r,\theta,\phi,r^2)$ has unit basis vectors
\begin{align*}
    v_r &= (\cos(\theta)\sin(\phi), \sin(\theta)\sin(\phi), \cos(\phi), 2r)\cdot\frac{1}{(4r^2+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}},\\
    v_\theta &= (-\sin(\theta), \cos(\theta), 0, 0),\\
    v_\phi &= (\cos(\theta)\cos(\phi), \sin(\theta)\cos(\phi), -\sin(\phi), 0).
\end{align*}
The shape operator in this basis is then given by the diagonal matrix
\begin{align*}
    S_{N(\zeta)}=\begin{pmatrix}
        -\frac{2}{(4r^2+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}} & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & -\frac{2}{(4r^2+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}} & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & -\frac{2}{(4r^2+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}

For fixed $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ checking the condition \eqref{curvad} amounts to establishing 
\begin{equation} \label{curvda3}
|\langle S_{N(\zeta_i)} v, v \rangle| \gtrsim \nu_i |v|^2, 
\end{equation}
$\forall v \in T_{\zeta_i} S_i$ with the property $v \perp N_j, j \in \{1,2,3\} \setminus \{ i \}$, for some choice of normals $N_j$ at the surfaces $S_j$. 

If $i=1,2$ then we see that 
\[
|\langle S_{N(\zeta_i)} v, v \rangle| \approx |v|^2,
\]
because in the support of $S_1,S_2$ we have $|r| \lesssim 1$. Thus we obtain \eqref{curvda3} with $\nu_1 \approx \nu_2 \approx 1$. 

Consider now the case $i=3$. If $M \approx 1$, then the same argument above applies. If $M \gg 1$ then we argue as follows. We pick $v \in T_{\zeta_3} S_3$ as detailed in \eqref{curvda3} and make the observation that since $v \perp N_j, j=1,2$ for some choices of normals $N_j$ to $S_j$, it follows that if $v=c_r v_r + c_\theta v_\theta + c_\phi v_\phi$, then we have $|c_\theta| + |c_\phi| \gtrsim |c_r|$. Indeed, if this were not the case, that is $|c_\theta| + |c_\phi| \ll |c_r|$, then using the fact that $r \gg 1$ and $N_1=\frac{(-2 \xi,1)}{\sqrt{1+4\xi^2}}$, it follows that
$|v_r \cdot N_1| \gtrsim 1$ and from this we obtain
\[
|v \cdot N_1| \gtrsim |c_r| |v_r \cdot N_1| \gtrsim 1,
\]
thus $v$ cannot be orthogonal to any normal $N_1$ at $S_1$. Using that $|c_\theta| + |c_\phi| \gtrsim |c_r|$ we then conclude
\[
|\langle S_{N(\zeta_3)} v, v \rangle| \approx r^{-3} |c_r|^2 + r^{-1}(|c_\theta|^2 + |c_\phi|^2) \gtrsim r^{-1} |v|^2.
\]
Thus we obtain \eqref{curvda3} with $\nu_3 \approx 2^{-k}$.

label: lci
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lci}
If P is a polynomial on $\mathbb{R}^n$, then for almost every $c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, $Z(P+c_0)$ is a transverse complete intersection.
More generally, suppose that $Z(P_1,...,P_{m})$ is a transverse complete intersection and that $P$ is another polynomial. Then for almost every $c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, 
$Z(P_1,...,P_{m},P+c_0)$ is a complete transverse intersection.

label: PP
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{PP}
Suppose that $W \geq 0$ is a non-zero $L^1$ function on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then, for any degree $D $ the following holds:

There is a sequence of polynomials $Q_1,...,Q_S$, with $\sum_{s=1}^S \operatorname{deg} Q_s \lesssim D$ and $2^S \approx D^n$, satisfying the following properties.
Let $P=\prod_{s=1}^S \tilde Q_s= \prod_{s=1}^S (Q_s+c_s)$ where $c_s \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $O_i$ be the open sets given by the sign conditions of $\tilde Q_s$, that is
\[
O_i=\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n| \operatorname{sign}(\tilde Q_s(x))=\sigma_s \}
\]
where $\sigma_s \in \{-1,+1\}$. There are $2^S \approx D^n$ cells $O_i$ and $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus Z(P)=\bigcup_i O_i$. 

If the constants $c_s$ are sufficiently small, then for every $O_i$ 
\[
\int_{O_i} W \approx D^{-n} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} W.
\]

title: Proof
body_md: Essentially the same iteration argument works as in the additive case using the polynomial ham sandwich theorem. The only difference is that at each step in the iteration we use the subadditivity $\mu(\mathbb{R}^n) \leq \mu(O)+\mu(O^c)$ and the bisection property $\mu(O)=\mu(O^c)$ to deduce that $\mu(O) \geq \frac12 \mu(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $\mu(O^c) \geq \frac12 \mu(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This is then carried through  every step in the iteration and leads to the desired conclusion.

label: aux111b
title: Proof
body_md:
We first remark that is suffices to establish the (apparently) stronger estimate
\begin{equation} \label{aux111b}
\left( \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \| \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\frac{2}{n-2}(P \cap Q_R)}^{\frac2{n-1}} \right)^{\frac{n-1}2}  
\lesssim  R^{\frac{n-1}2}  C(\bm{\nu}) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \| f_{i} \|_{L^2(U_i)}.
\end{equation}
We start with the generic estimate
\[
\| \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\frac{2}{n-2}(P)} \lesssim  C(\bm{\nu}) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \| f_{i} \|_{L^2(U_i)}.
\]
It is standard that this estimate localizes, in that it suffices to consider the relevant masses within the parallelepiped $P$; precisely we have
\begin{equation} \label{aux111a}
\| \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\frac{2}{n-2}(P)} \lesssim  C(\bm{\nu}) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \left(\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}_i} \langle z_i \rangle^{-N} \| \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\infty_{x_i} L^2_{\bar x_i}(P+ \nu_i^{-1} z_i)} \right),
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}_i= \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^n: z_i=0 \}$. For fixed $i$, we have the estimate
\[
\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}: c_i(P)=constant} \left(\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}_i} \langle z_i \rangle^{-N} \| \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\infty_{x_i} L^2_{\bar x_i}(P+ \nu_i^{-1} z_i)} \right)^2 \lesssim \| \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\infty_{x_i} L^2_{\bar x_i}}^2 \lesssim \|f_{i}\|_{L^2},
\]
where we recall that $c(P)$ is the center of the parallelepiped $P$. The above is a consequence of the fact that the mass of $\mathcal E_i f_{i}$ within parallelepipeds $P$ with $c_i(P)=constant$ has good orthogonality properties, which in turn is a consequence of the dispersive properties of the operator $\mathcal E_i$. From this last estimate we obtain
\[
\begin{split}
& \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}: P \subset Q_R} \left(\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}_i} \langle z_i \rangle^{-N} \| \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\infty_{x_i} L^2_{\bar x_i}(P+ \nu_i^{-1} z_i)} \right)^2 \\
\lesssim & R^\frac12 \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}: c_i(P)=constant} \left(\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}_i} \langle z_i \rangle^{-N} \| \mathcal E_i f_{i} \|_{L^\infty_{x_i} L^2_{\bar x_i}(P+ \nu_i^{-1} z_i)} \right)^2 \\
\lesssim &  R^\frac12 \|f_{i}\|_{L^2}. 
\end{split}
\]
From this and \eqref{aux111a} we obtain \eqref{aux111b}.

\label{lsc}
Let $\mathcal{Q}\subseteq \mathcal{P}$ be a collection of parallelepipeds in $\mathcal{P}$ and let $N\geq 1$. Then there exists $O(N\#\mathcal{Q}^{\frac{1}{N}})$ many sparse collections $\mathcal{O}_l\subseteq \mathcal{P}_{R_l}$ which cover $\mathcal{Q}$ such that $1\lesssim R_l\lesssim \#\mathcal{Q}^{C^N}$.
